2.text: “And from the Cape to that Island it is possible to go in the summer-

3.text: time in one day, in a baidara with oars; and in the wintertime, with reindeer,

4.text: also in one day. Upon this island are game of every kind, sables and martens,

5.text: foxes, polar foxes, wolves, wolverenes, polar bears, marine beavers (sea-otters).

6.text: They feed on sea-game, roots and berries, and weeds. Upon this island also

7.text: are trees of every kind, — cedar, pine, fir, larch. And the wood of those

8.text: island trees they (Peter and his comrades) have seen in the houses, on the

9.text: baidaras and canoes of those Chukchee. And those island people live in the

10.text: same way as the Chukchee, and they have no authorities. And on the Cape

11.text: there are no peltries besides wolves and red foxes, and even those are few,

12.text: because there is no wood at all. And these Chukchee, Reindeer and walking

13.text: [sedentary] have bow-men, approximately about two thousand, besides those

14.text: of the Anadyr River, who have fifty bow-men and more. As to the island

15.text: people, Makachkin and the captive islanders said to him, to Peter and his

16.text: comrades, ‘They are three times as numerous as the Chukchee;’ and he

17.text: (Makachkin) has been visiting that island on war-expeditions during many

18.text: years. And the Chukchee call that island a large land.”¹

19.text: This description of polar America adjacent to Bering Sea is quite clear

20.text: and detailed. One must not forget that it was made seventeen years earlier

21.text: than the voyage of Bering. “(Large-) toothed” is evidently a translation of

22.text: the Chukchee “(large-) mouthed” (yɪkɪrg̣aˊulɪt).² Semen Deshnev, in his reports

23.text: of 1648, also mentions the (large-) toothed men living on two small islands,

24.text: evidently on the Diomede Islands. Not without interest is the mention of the

25.text: River Chukchee of the Anadyr, Nokon and his comrades, who paid tribute for

26.text: five men. Up to the present time the River Chukchee of the Middle Anadyr

27.text: pay about the same amount of tribute. Much in use among them is the

28.text: name “Nikon.” This name is of Greek origin, and belongs to the Greek-

29.text: Orthodox calendar; but it may have some connection with the name “Nokon”

30.text: of the beginning of the eighteenth century.

31.text: From all this information it may be seen that the war against the

32.text: Chukchee was carried on almost without interruption, and certainly without

33.text: mercy. The Chukchee, however, in this respect, did not remain behind the

35.text: I collected in the village Pokhotsk, on the Lower Kolyma, several

36.text: interesting tales of the inroads and raids of the Chukchee against the Russian

37.text: settlements on both the Kolyma and the Anadyr. Pokhotsk, for example, is

38.text: a large village at the western mouth of the Kolyma. It is inhabited by the

39.text: descendants of the ancient Cossacks, who in 1876 were transferred to the

40.text: burghess class (мѣщане). The former Cossack race has preserved itself in

41.text: that village comparatively in its purest form. The tales probably refer to the
